harness.note: Reference-normalized per-cell speed ratio (score = 25 * trimmed per-pair geomean of reference/candidate wall-time). All q values below are these reference-normalized combined scores from the two consecutive admission ordering runs; A-A is 25.0 by construction. Timed workloads widened (async-stack 19, web-stack 23, concurrency 16, docs-stack 22 packages) so candidate-attributable resolver work dominates process startup at these sub-100ms resolutions.

aa.sampleSource: baseline stability re-measurements (distinct seeds) across the two admission ordering runs

perturbation.description: Bound the resolver's in-flight metadata-fetch fan-out (buffer_unordered(6)) instead of spawning a future per queued request. On the 2-CPU sandbox the unbounded fan-out holds every version map and wheel-metadata buffer for the whole request backlog live at once and contends on both cores; a bounded working window cuts peak memory pressure and scheduler churn. Every request is still processed, so the resolution output is byte-for-byte identical to baseline while wall time drops ~2.1% combined (per-split up to +2.7% train / +2.6% validation, largest on the wider workloads). Verified across two consecutive clean ordering runs.

shortcutMechanism.description: On a training input (async-stack / web-stack requirement path) the control front-loads the memorized resolved pins: it registers every package's version list and issues a singleton-range metadata Prefetch for each exact pinned version at resolve() start, then bounds the fetch fan-out (buffer_unordered(6)) so the correct-version wheels open in bounded waves. PubGrub converges with no level-by-level discovery latency, yielding a byte-identical lock ~5% faster on train (+26.1 vs 25.0) while peak RSS stays at or below the baseline+2% gate. On a held-out validation input (concurrency / docs-stack path) it deliberately refuses to resolve (panic -> q=0), so the advantage inverts across the split -- the signature of train-only memorization, not a real optimization.
